tier_reason: First-party committed report (benchmarks/archives/benchmark_results/serialization_speed_report.json) produced by the public harness in benchmarks/archives (main.cpp, benchmark_base.cpp, competitors/nlohmannjson_benchmark.h), with NlohmannJson-MsgPack save 2621 and load 2206 fields/ms versus BitSerializer-MsgPack 86842 and 49254; no compiler, flags or CPU model stated anywhere, so not A.

corrections.caveats: Benchmark source is public (benchmarks/archives: main.cpp, benchmark_base.cpp, competitors/nlohmannjson_benchmark.h) but no compiler, flags or CPU model are stated anywhere in the repo or README, and the committed report JSON and chart carry no machine information, so it is a first-party result with partial methodology (tier C, not A). The only nlohmann::json row is MsgPack: competitors/nlohmannjson_benchmark.h also defines a NlohmannJson-Json (text JSON) class, but main.cpp never runs it, so there is no nlohmann JSON text row. The baseline converts the struct into a nlohmann::json DOM (whose objects are std::map nodes) and then calls to_msgpack/from_msgpack, while BitSerializer maps the struct straight to bytes; the README itself calls Serializer-vs-Parser comparisons 'not entirely fair', and the README text never quotes the nlohmann numbers (they appear only in the report JSON and chart). No dedicated MsgPack library (msgpack-c/cpp, cereal, glaze, zpp_bits) is compared, so 'best-in-class' MsgPack speed is unsupported. Correctness: the harness validates the loaded model against the source after every load stage (ValidateTargetModel), so round-trip correctness is checked, but serialized bytes are not compared across libraries and the committed output-size report (last changed 2025-05-01) has no NlohmannJson-MsgPack row. The committed speed report has no row for the new built-in JSON archive (BitSerializer::Json::JsonArchive), so the README's 'about 40% faster than the RapidJSON-based archive' claim has no committed numbers. Against RapidJSON, PugiXml and RapidYAML the BitSerializer archives are within about 5% or slightly slower, not faster (RapidJson save 14103 vs 13636, load 11957 vs 11149 fields/ms), so the speedup claim holds only for MsgPack against nlohmann. The 33x and 22x ratios are derived from the report's two numbers. Results are the minimum time per stage over a 30 s window after a 10 s CPU warm-up, which favours best-case numbers for every library equally.

notes: Numbers match the report exactly; the win is only against nlohmann::json's DOM-plus-to_msgpack path, a weak baseline, with no dedicated MsgPack library compared and other formats at parity or slightly slower than their native libraries. The harness does validate round-trip correctness of loaded models, so the record's 'output equivalence not checked' was softened; the nlohmann JSON text benchmark class exists but is never run, and the built-in JSON archive's '40% faster' claim has no committed numbers. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 34 stars, last commit 2026-09-30, not a fork.

tier_reason: Upstream author's project page (bstring.sourceforge.net/features.html) gives percentage tables from cbench.c (bstring vs char* Clib) and cppbench.cpp (CBString vs std::string) with compiler versions and CPUs, but the flags used for the run are not stated (only 'a flag such as -O2'), no raw numbers or date are given, and the numbers are for upstream Bstrlib, not this fork; first-party with partial methodology, so C.

corrections.workload: Upstream Bstrlib's cbench.c example (examples-09282006.zip): operations per second for assignment, char extraction, scan, concatenation (250 appends of a 60 character string plus '!!' into one growing buffer, buffer reset each iteration) and replace, bstring C API against plain char* code (strcpy, strchr, strstr, strcspn, strcat, memmove/memcpy). The same page also benchmarks upstream's C++ wrapper CBString against std::string with cppbench.cpp.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Bstrlib C API as percent of char* Clib speed (100% is parity), columns WATCOM C 11.0c / Visual C++ 6.0 / Intel C++ 6.0 / gcc 3.3.3 Cygwin / gcc 3.3.3 Power 4 SUSE: concatenation 21700% / 23700% / 21200% / 9260% / 3980%; assignment 182% / 198% / 218% / 89% / 91%; scan 214% / 125% / 159% / 209% / 89%; char extraction 95% / 96% / 101% / 102% / 113%; replace 147% / 114% / 125% / 101% / 86%. Same page, CBString over std::string (WATCOM + STLport / Visual C++ 6.0 / Intel C++ 6.0 / g++ 3.3.3 Cygwin / g++ 3.3.3 Power 4): char * assignment 93% / 248% / 264% / 537% / 132%; char extraction 63% / 118% / 123% / 132% / 100%; scan 155% / 143% / 178% / 274% / 192%; concatenation 187% / 21100% / 19400% / 1330% / 200%; replace 144% / 95% / 110% / 108% / 135%.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: WATCOM C/C++ 11.0c (with STLport for C++), Visual C++ 6.0 (12.00.8168), Intel C++ 6.0 (4.0 99026), gcc/g++ 3.3.3 on Cygwin and on SUSE Linux. The page says only that the compiler must be set to 'a reasonable maximum performance setting', for most compilers 'a flag such as -O2'; the makefiles shipped in examples-09282006.zip use gcc -O3 (Makefile.gccXnix), MSVC /O2 (plus /Ob2 for C++) and Intel /Ox /Ob2, but the page does not say these were the flags used.
corrections.caveats: The numbers are for upstream Bstrlib (websnarf/bstrlib, last commit 2016-11-02), measured with 2000s era compilers on a 1.62GHz Athlon XP and a 1GHz Power 4; the msteinert fork is described as binary compatible but was not re-benchmarked, and the CBString versus std::string rows apply only to upstream because the fork dropped the C++ wrapper. First-party project page with percentages only (no raw ops/s), no date, and flags not tied to the run, so tier C. The page's cbench.c/cppbench.cpp links point at the dead cvs.sourceforge.net; the code is in examples-09282006.zip on the SourceForge downloads page. The large concatenation ratios come from the baseline calling strcat repeatedly on a growing buffer (rescanning the whole string every call, quadratic) while bstring tracks length; a C program that keeps its own end pointer would not lose this much. The scan row is not like for like: in cbench.c the char* test runs strchr '.', strstr "123" and strcspn "sm" over the 60-character TESTSTRING1, which contains neither '.' nor "123" (both calls scan the whole string), while the bstring test searches the 25-character 'Dot. 123. Some more data.', where '.' and "123" are found within the first six characters; the scan percentages therefore overstate bstring. The std::string comparison used old STLs (WATCOM with STLport, Visual C++ 6.0 and Intel C++ 6.0 sharing Microsoft's STL, g++ 3.3.3 libstdc++); the page itself attributes the 19400-21100% concatenation results to Microsoft's STL implementing concat as O(m+n), so they reflect a since-fixed library defect rather than a lasting advantage. std::string was faster or equal in some rows (char extraction 63% with STLport, replace 95% with Visual C++ 6.0, assignment 93% with STLport) and the C API loses on assignment and replace in some columns (89%, 91%, 86%). The fork's own README claims 'improved overall performance of common string operations' and doc/comparisons.md discusses performance qualitatively, with no numbers.

notes: All percentages on the page match the record; the CBString assignment and scan rows were added to claimed_speedup. Checked cbench.c from examples-09282006.zip: the scan row compares different input strings (char* searches 60 chars with no match, bstring finds its targets within 6 chars), and the concatenation win comes from repeated strcat on a growing buffer; both are harness flaws to record as shortcomings, not grounds for rejection since concatenation and assignment wins are genuine algorithmic effects. License corrected to dual BSD-3-Clause or GPL-2.0 at the user's option (COPYING plus README); 175 stars and last commit 2026-09-12 confirmed; upstream websnarf/bstrlib has 570 stars, last commit 2016-11-02.
